strengths: the authors consider an import problem statement, which is a very natural generalisation of the SBM problem
the proposed approach is theoretically sound
the authors test their approach on a diverse set of problems
the text is easy to follow
The authors exposit their work quite well (with adjustments needed mentioned in the weaknesses and questions section).
The experimental section is thorough and highlights the myriad applications of the perspectives presented in the paper.

With the proper contextualization, the method presented is interesting and falls in line well with a series of other related works, highlighting the benefits of controllable paths (for the limited set of potentials the consider).
The paper presents a method which improves upon previous methods by ensuring guaranteed feasibility and stronger performance in high dimension.
The method also seems to clearly outperform comparable methods in the various application settings.
The paper has rigorous logic, clear expression and abundant experimental details.

This work broadens the scope of application of Schrodinger bridge matching (SBM) algorithm and converts the existing optimal transport mapping and SBM methods into the special case of variational formulas.
In addition, the feasibility conditions are met at any time during the entire training process, which is a big difference from the previous methods.
Overall, this work opens up new algorithmic opportunities for training diffusion models with task-specific optimal structures.
weaknesses: the authors did not investigate computational limits of the proposed approach
it seems that the proposed approach does not work in case of image data, only if we consider some latent space like in sec. 4.2. Any ideas how we can improve here?

While the experiments are cool and thorough, and while the framing of the optimization problem is coherent, the paper diminishes itself by its framing... the framing issue is that it oversells itself in a way that misleads the reader.
The paper does not provide a numerical solution to optimal transport or the Schrödinger Bridge, yet it casts OT and SB as edge-cases of their variational problem, overstating its contributions.

Constraint (6b) is quite hard to enforce; the Gaussian approximation may be insufficient, and the authors should be careful in stating what it is they are doing and how it relates to the problem they are seeking to solve.
The primary cited work (Flow Matching for Generative Modeling) also specifies an 'optimal transport path' that does not actually provide a means to solve OT.
Overstating the ability to solve OT/SB can mislead new readers and cause confusion in the field.
The paper should tone down its claims and include caveats about the approximate nature of the method.
The discussion about feasibility seems not so useful; the problem statement assumes feasibility, making the comparison less relevant.
There are semantically inexact statements, e.g., misuse of the word 'comparison' when describing gradient field matching probability densities.
The paper should acknowledge that optimal transport considers a variety of costs beyond the W2 cost.
The experiments do not convincingly demonstrate a distinct coupling; initial and final empirical densities appear identical.
The convergence guarantees obtained are merely local, and do not guarantee convergence to a global optimum.
The method requires a differentiable state cost.
The GSBM method requires the differentiability of V_t and is not applicable to any form of V_t.
The method relies on quadratic control costs to establish its convergence analysis, limiting the scope of theoretical results.
The paper does not fully explore the implications of the restriction to quadratic control costs on practical applicability, especially for non-quadratic costs.
The differentiability requirement of V_t may restrict the types of state costs that can be used, excluding non-smooth or discontinuous V_t.
